implementation_notes: Resolve rt_id_actress, us_code, f_code by linear scan of dict offsets/data.
Step 1: parallel scan name/gender.bin and name/name.{off,dat}; collect pids (1-based row id = i+1) where gender==f_code and name substring contains 'Angel'.
Step 2: for each pid, lo=cipid_off[pid], hi=cipid_off[pid+1]; iterate r in [lo,hi).
Step 3: check ci.role_id[r]==rt_id_actress; check ci.note offset length == 7 && memcmp('(voice)',7)==0; check ci.person_role_id[r] != INT32_MIN.
Step 4: mv = ci.movie_id[r]; require title.production_year[mv-1] in [2007,2010].

Step 5: iterate mc rows in [mc_off[mv], mc_off[mv+1]); for each, check note LIKE '%(200%)%' AND (LIKE '%(USA)%' OR LIKE '%(worldwide)%') AND cn.country_code[mc.company_id[k]-1]==us_code. If any match, mark movie qualified.
Step 6: chn_id = ci.person_role_id[r]; candidate char_name name at row chn_id-1.
Step 7: iterate aka_name range [aka_off[pid], aka_off[pid+1]); if non-empty, candidate aka name = min over range; require non-empty for join.
Step 8: update 4 MINs only when full match found. Use thread-local MIN strings; final reduction picks lexicographic min.
LIKE matching: simple memmem / naive substring search on raw note bytes — patterns are short literals.
Memory budget: title.production_year ~10MB, cn.country_code ~470KB, ci CSR ~160MB (mmap), mc offsets ~10MB, aka offsets ~16MB. Well within 62GB.
